name: HyperMem

paper.title: HyperMem: Hypergraph Memory for Long-Term Conversations

construction.unit: episode (dialogue segment with title, summary and third-person narrative) + facts
construction.kept_as: LLM-rewritten episode narrative and summary; extracted fact sentences; raw turns kept
construction.processing: LLM boundary detector cuts the stream into episodes; LLM writes title, summary and narrative; facts extracted per topic
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4.1-mini in the released config)

organization.structure: three-level hypergraph: topics → episodes → facts; a topic is a weighted hyperedge over its episodes, an episode a weighted hyperedge over its facts
organization.stores: topic, episode and fact nodes with BM25 and dense indexes
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-4B dense (embeddings propagated through hyperedges, λ = 0.5) + BM25

management.operations: LLM matches each new episode against existing topics: joins and regenerates matched topics, or starts a new one

retrieval.candidates: BM25 + dense fused by RRF at each level: topics, then episodes of the chosen topics, then facts of the chosen episodes
retrieval.selection: top-10 topics, top-10 episodes, top-30 facts; paper adds Qwen3-Reranker-4B at each level (off by default in the released code)

use.context: episode narratives with timestamps + fact sentences with time and place

classify.note: The paper reranks each level with Qwen3-Reranker-4B; the released code turns the reranker off by default, so the top-k of the RRF list decides.

stages.ingestion: Messages stream into a buffer; an LLM boundary detector decides after each new message whether the buffer forms a complete episode (topic change, time gap, closing signals).
stages.construction: Each episode gets an LLM-written title, 2-4 sentence summary and a detailed third-person narrative with absolute dates; the raw turns are kept. Facts (a sentence, the questions it could answer, keywords, an importance weight) are later extracted per topic and anchored to their source episodes.
stages.organization: Topics group episodes through weighted episode hyperedges; each episode groups its facts through a weighted fact hyperedge. Node embeddings are shifted towards their hyperedges' weighted means (h' = h + 0.5·Σ h_e).
stages.update: The LLM compares a new episode with all existing topics (10 per call); matched topics absorb it and get a regenerated title and summary, otherwise a new topic is created. An episode can join several topics.
stages.retrieval: Coarse to fine: BM25 + dense RRF over topics keeps 10, RRF over those topics' episodes keeps 10, RRF over those episodes' facts keeps 30. The paper reranks each level with Qwen3-Reranker-4B over 100 RRF candidates.
stages.answer: GPT-4.1-mini answers with a step-by-step prompt from the 10 episode narratives and 30 facts; topic text is not included.

summary: Conversation memory as a three-level hypergraph (topics over episodes over facts) with hyperedge-smoothed embeddings, read top-down from topics to episodes to facts.
notes: Venue: ACL 2026 long paper (aclanthology 2026.acl-long.1627), matching the arXiv comment 'ACL 2026 Main'. The paper says code is 'about to be released'; the official repo EverMind-AI/HyperMem (linked from EverOS's README) was checked at commit 15c70090 (2026-06-03). HyperMem shares its episode prompt design with EverMemOS (same group, EverMind AI).

sources.code_note: Repo created 2026-06-02, about two months after paper v2; 6 commits, head 15c70090. The run script defaults (reranker off, top-k 10/10/30) and the README (top-k 15/25/30) disagree with each other and with the paper (reranker on), so exact identity with the paper's runs is not guaranteed. Episode detection (stage 1) is not in the default run script, which starts from stage 2.

abstract.text: HyperMem argues that pairwise links in RAG and graph memories miss joint relations among several pieces of a long conversation. It stores memory as a hypergraph with three levels: topics, episodes (contiguous dialogue segments) and facts, where hyperedges group all episodes of a topic and all facts of an episode. Embeddings are smoothed along hyperedges and indexed with BM25, and retrieval narrows from topics to episodes to facts. On LoCoMo the authors report 92.73% LLM-judge accuracy, above RAG and memory-system baselines.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: The answer model reads LLM-written episode narratives plus extracted facts; topic text and raw turns are not included.
Topics only route: the answer comes from episodes and facts inside the 10 chosen topics, each level re-scored from the question alone.
Removing episode context costs the most (92.66 → 88.90); skipping topic retrieval costs 0.72 points.

open_questions: Only one benchmark (LoCoMo) is used, and all hyperparameter sweeps are on that same test set.
The ablation does not separate hyperedge embedding propagation from the rest; λ = 0 still gives 91.69 vs 92.66 (Fig. 4).

discussion.takeaway: Grouping a conversation into topics, episodes and facts linked by hyperedges, and reading it top-down, gives the highest LoCoMo score in the paper (92.73), mostly thanks to returning whole episode narratives alongside facts.

claims.claim: State of the art on LoCoMo.
claims.evidence: 92.73 overall vs 86.49 HyperGraphRAG and 85.38 MIRIX. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Hyperedges bind scattered episodes for multi-hop questions.
claims.evidence: multi-hop 93.62 vs 84.04 LightRAG; facts-only retrieval loses 5.68 on multi-hop. Table 1, §4.3

claims.claim: Episode context is the most important component.
More accurate and cheaper than graph RAG.
claims.evidence: 92.73 at 7.5x Mem0 tokens vs GraphRAG 67.60 at 35.3x and HyperGraphRAG 86.49 at 26.3x. Fig. 5

limits: Assumes a single user; multi-user or multi-agent memory raises access-control and isolation issues.
Open-domain questions stay hard because they need knowledge beyond the conversation.
reading: Memory-system baselines are copied from other papers (Mem0, MIRIX, MemOS) that used other answer models: the Mem0-sourced rows used GPT-4o-mini while HyperMem uses GPT-4.1-mini, and MIRIX's source judged with GPT-4.1, not the GPT-4o-mini the caption states.
The best result (92.73) and the ablation baseline (92.66) come from slightly different top-k settings; λ and top-k were tuned on LoCoMo itself, the only benchmark.

Topics only select which episodes are searched: their text never reaches the answer model, and episode and fact scores do not use the topic score or the hyperedge weights (code stage4 L680-L710, L795-L825).

Skipping topic retrieval costs 0.72 points, while dropping episode narratives costs 3.76, so most of the gain comes from giving the answer model rewritten episodes, much as in EverMemOS from the same group.
BM25 at the episode and fact levels scores the whole conversation and keeps only hits inside the chosen set (top 2k), so it can contribute few candidates.
The released code has no reranker by default and a question-type 'temporal enhancement' flag that is computed but unused; which settings produced Table 1 cannot be checked.
The repo README reprints Table 1 with a few different baseline cells (OpenAI open-domain 63.22 vs 62.29, LangMem 72.20 vs 71.12, MemU 50.56 vs 50.01).
